title: Build your first retro material
text: CrowPSX is a shader and material-authoring suite for Unity's Built-in Render Pipeline and Universal Render Pipeline. This manual covers installation, shader controls, scene setup, and troubleshooting for version 1.1.0 .  If you're new to the package, follow these three steps:  Install and validate. Keep the package at Assets/CrowPSX and run the installation validator. Installation → Make one material. Choose Default, Lite, or PBR, assign a texture, then tune lighting and retro geometry. Getting started → Build out the scene. Add foliage, terrain, particles, decals, and a procedural sky using the matching shader families. Shader reference →

title: Choose your path
text: I want to… Start here Check my Unity and render pipeline setup Pipeline compatibility Tune vertex snapping, affine warp, or lighting Lighting & retro controls Work with packed textures or roughness maps PBR workflows Paint multiple materials onto one mesh Vertex painting Apply settings across many materials Material Manager Fix pink materials, decals, or outlines Troubleshooting

title: What is included?
text: Surface, vertex-painting, and Nature shaders each offer Default, Lite, and PBR variants. The suite also includes Terrain PBR, Standard and Grab Distortion particles, depth-volume decals, and a procedural skybox.  The inspector exposes controls supported by the selected shader. A control absent from one variant is not necessarily missing from the package. See each family reference for its supported workflow.

title: Before you begin
text: Use Unity 2022.3 LTS or newer with Built-in or URP. HDRP shaders are not included. Polybrush and Bakery are optional. For exact version and renderer details, read pipeline compatibility .  The documentation is built from the CrowPSX 1.1.0 package manuals. Product screenshots elsewhere on this site show authored demo scenes; the resulting appearance also depends on your meshes, textures, lighting, and camera presentation.

title: Overview
text: Understand the suite and find the right guide for your task.

title: Requirements
text: Unity 2022.3 LTS or newer, tested on 2022.3, 6.0, 6.3 and 6.6 Built-in Render Pipeline or Universal Render Pipeline (Forward, Forward+ and, on Unity 6.6, Deferred+), HDRP shaders are not included Shader Model 3.5-capable target for the main surface, particle, and decal shaders Installed as a conventional Asset Store package, not a UPM package. It must stay at Assets/CrowPSX Polybrush and Bakery are both optional The demo scene uses Unity UI, and runs under the Input Manager, the Input System, or both

title: Import the package
text: Import the complete Assets/CrowPSX folder and leave it at that path. Run Tools > CrowPSX > Validate Installation . Create a material and choose a shader from the CrowPSX menu.  See Getting Started for the first material, and Demo Scene for the playable scene at Assets/CrowPSX/Demo.unity .

title: Validate the installation
text: Run Tools > CrowPSX > Validate Installation after import and after changing render pipelines. The validator checks shader discovery, required package contents, shader properties, assembly placement, and relevant URP renderer setup. It reports issues without changing project settings or material assets.  Wait for compilation to finish before judging missing shaders or inspector controls. If Unity reports an error, start with the first relevant Console message and use the troubleshooting guide .

title: Open the included demo
text: Open Assets/CrowPSX/Demo.unity . The demo works with the Input Manager, Input System, or both. Its documented controls and sample scripts are covered in Demo scene .

title: Next step
text: Create a material using CrowPSX/Surface/Lite or CrowPSX/Surface/Default , assign a Base Texture, and apply it to a mesh. Continue with Getting started for lighting, geometry, and rendering controls.

title: Installation
text: Requirements, package import, installation checks, and the included demo.

title: 1. Import and validate
text: Import the complete Assets/CrowPSX folder, leave it at that path, and wait for Unity to finish compiling. Run:  Tools > CrowPSX > Validate Installation  The validator checks shader discovery, the shader property contract, XR tokens in the shared includes, editor assembly placement, required package contents, the property catalog used by CrowPSX tools, and (under the Universal Render Pipeline) whether the active Universal Renderer carries the CrowPSX Depth Volume feature. It never changes project settings or material assets.  To inspect the complete package, open Assets/CrowPSX/Demo.unity . See Demo Scene for controls and input requirements.

title: 2. Choose a shader
text: Create a Unity material and select a shader from the CrowPSX menu.  Surface/Default : full stylized non-PBR feature set Surface/Lite : reduced surface shader for simpler materials Surface/PBR : separate or packed PBR maps, normal, metallic, ambient occlusion, height parallax, smoothness/roughness, specular, reflections, and detail maps Surface/Vertex Painting/... : dedicated four-layer materials driven by mesh vertex colors Nature/... : cutout-friendly Default, Lite, and PBR foliage shaders with wind deformation Terrain/PBR : Terrain material using Unity TerrainLayers, with CrowPSX lighting, color, and pixel-snap controls Particles : ParticleSystem-oriented VFX shaders Decals/Depth Volume : projected box-volume decal Skybox/Procedural : procedural environment shader

title: 3. Set up a Terrain material
text: Select the Terrain object, open Terrain Settings , set Material to Custom , then assign a material using CrowPSX/Terrain/PBR .  CrowPSX reads the Terrain's existing TerrainLayers, including their albedo, normal, metallic, smoothness, and holes data. In the Built-in Render Pipeline, Unity automatically uses the bundled supporting terrain passes for more than four layers and for the distant basemap; keep those hidden shaders in the original CrowPSX/Shaders/Terrain folder. Under the Universal Render Pipeline the same shader follows URP's own terrain contract and the hidden Built-in helpers are unused.

title: 4. Configure VR rendering
text: CrowPSX supports Multi-Pass, Single Pass Instanced, and Android Multiview in the Built-in Render Pipeline, and URP's Single Pass Instanced and Multiview modes.  Use the Forward rendering path for Single Pass Instanced. Built-in deferred does not support that mode. Soft particles and Depth Volume decals require the camera depth texture. Grab Distortion uses true scene refraction in Multi-Pass and a stereo-safe heat-ripple fallback in Single Pass Instanced/Multiview. Use VR / Stereo Comfort to choose a profile or tune VR Snap Strength and VR Affine Strength independently. Stereo snapping shares one displacement between both eyes to preserve binocular disparity.

title: 5. Set up the surface
text: Regular surface shaders use Base Texture and Base Color .  Painted variants use Painted Material Layers instead. Select Base, Red, Green, or Blue and assign the maps for that layer. Their regular _MainTex surface path is intentionally absent.  For a PBR material, choose Separate Maps when individual maps need different textures or UV transforms, or Packed Map to read Metallic, Ambient Occlusion, Height, and Smoothness/Roughness from one texture. Enable Link PBR UVs to drive all core PBR transforms from the surface-color texture. See PBR Workflows .

title: 6. Configure lighting
text: Open Lighting and choose:  Pixel for smoother per-pixel realtime lighting Vertex for a coarser retro or fixed-function appearance  Use Lighting Steps for quantized bands. Final Posterize grades the completed lit result rather than only the source texture.

title: 7. Configure retro geometry
text: Open Retro Geometry :  Pixel Snap X/Y controls screen-space snapping Affine Warp reduces perspective-correct texture interpolation Snap Fade Start/End reduces near-camera instability VR Snap Strength controls how much stereo-stable snapping remains in VR VR Affine Strength independently controls affine texture warping in VR Snap Shadow Caster applies compatible snapping in the shadow pass  The effect is vertex-dependent. Large triangles produce larger visible steps and affine distortion.

title: 8. Optional outlines
text: On a Default, Lite, PBR, or Vertex Painting material, open Outline and enable it. Choose fixed screen pixels or world-space width, optionally fade it over a camera-distance range, mask it with a texture, and use Match Base Color to blend toward the sampled surface. The outline is an extra draw only while enabled; disabling it switches the shader pass off. Prefer Opaque or Cutout because transparent surfaces normally do not write enough depth to hide their own hull. Nature is excluded because its usual single-plane alpha cards require texture-silhouette dilation rather than a closed-mesh hull.  If hard edges leave gaps in the hull, change Normal Source to Baked Smooth UV4 . Click Bake Outline Normals in the material inspector to bake the renderer shown in Source Renderer , or use Tools > CrowPSX > Outline Normals to bake across selected scene objects. The generated copy is saved beside the source model, preserves the original mesh shading, and uses UV4 only for continuous outline extrusion. Use the matching Restore action to reassign the source mesh later. Enable Read/Write in the model importer if the baker reports an unreadable mesh.  Source Renderer defaults to the selected object's renderer, so it only needs an assignment when baking a renderer other than the one being inspected. The bake always works in place: the generated mesh goes onto that renderer and the material keeps drawing its own outline pass. There is no separate outline renderer and no rendering-mode control.  Under URP, use the warning's Add CrowPSX Outline To Universal Renderer button once. URP requires that renderer feature to request the additional outline pass. Built-in rendering needs no setup.

title: 9. Choose a rendering mode
text: Open Rendering and choose:  Opaque for solid geometry Cutout for hard alpha silhouettes such as fences, leaves, cards, and grates Transparent for blended opacity  CrowPSX synchronizes blend state, render tags, queue behavior, and recommended depth settings when the rendering mode changes.

title: 10. Set up a Nature material
text: Choose CrowPSX/Nature/Lite , Default , or PBR for leaves, grass, vines, and similar foliage.  Assign the Albedo texture and keep Use Main Texture Alpha enabled. Nature shaders begin in Cutout mode with Cull Off . Open Nature Wind and apply the closest preset: Gentle Leaves, Grass Breeze, Shrub, Tree Canopy, or Strong Wind. Choose an Anchoring Source : Local Height for grass and plants with a ground-level pivot Vertex Alpha for authored per-vertex anchoring UV2 Y when the mesh stores a wind weight in its second UV channel Mask Texture for UV-authored control Adjust Maximum Bend first. Use low Sway/Gust frequencies for natural movement, then add Leaf Flutter sparingly. Verify realtime shadows. Baked shadows use the mesh rest pose.

title: 11. Use presets
text: General Presets provides console-era and practical starting points. Custom presets are shared by the material inspector and Material Manager and saved to:  ProjectSettings/CrowPSX/CustomMaterialPresets.json

title: 12. Batch-edit materials
text: Open:  Tools > CrowPSX > Material Manager  Use it to copy compatible settings, reset groups, convert surface variants, apply presets, batch-change rendering and lighting, or apply a VR comfort profile to many materials. Review the target list before applying project-wide operations.

title: 13. Configure a procedural sky
text: Assign a material using CrowPSX/Skybox/Procedural in Lighting > Environment > Skybox Material .  Use the sky gradient and final grading controls for the environment base. Environment Lighting keeps Lighting > Environment Lighting > Source set to Skybox. Filter Skybox Ambient Color optionally reduces or tints the generated ambient probe without recoloring the visible sky or its reflections, Auto Apply To Active Scene pushes changes as you edit, and Apply To Scene applies them once on demand. The filter affects the realtime fallback probe; rebake lightmaps and baked Light Probes to pick up a revised environment color. Enable the Sun, Moon, or extra celestial bodies as needed. Celestial masks can use Texture Alpha, Brightness, or Alpha × Brightness. Enable Moon Phase for an analytic lunar cycle with phase presets, terminator controls, and earthshine. Stars follow spherical latitude rings. Amount controls population; Size and Brightness remain independent. Cloud self-lighting follows the strongest enabled Sun or Moon above the horizon. HDR exposure and celestial highlights remain unclamped for bloom, reflection probes, and environment capture; tone mapping belongs to the camera/output pipeline.

title: 14. Set up depth-volume decals
text: Depth-volume decals rebuild the receiving surface from the camera depth texture, so the rendering camera has to produce one, and the decal volume has to intersect opaque geometry.  Under the Universal Render Pipeline they also need the CrowPSX Depth Volume renderer feature on the active Universal Renderer; without it URP hands the decal last frame's depth or a vertex-snapped surface and the decal drifts or flickers as the camera moves. Select the decal material and use the inspector's Add To Renderer action, or add it manually with Add Renderer Feature > CrowPSX Depth Volume .  Most surfaces require no stencil setup. To prevent decals on a particular material:  Set the surface material's Optional Stencil / Decal Masking preset to Block Decals . Set the depth-volume decal material to Respect Blockers . Use Receiver and Test Receivers only when an explicit allow-list is required.  Blocker and receiver flags use separate stencil bits and can coexist on the same material.

title: Recommended first checks
text: Verify the material in Scene and Game views. Test the intended realtime-lighting mode. Confirm rendering mode, queue, and Z Write behavior. Test one baked-lighting setup if the project uses lightmaps. Import PBR normal textures as Normal Map . Import manually authored packed PBR maps with sRGB disabled. Start Parallax Height near zero and increase it gradually while checking grazing angles. Confirm painted meshes contain vertex colors and enough vertices for the desired brush resolution. Back up the project before performing a project-wide material operation.

title: Getting started
text: Create your first material and configure lighting, geometry, and rendering.

title: Built-in and URP
text: Every lit CrowPSX shader ships both a Universal and a Built-in SubShader in the same asset, and Unity picks the one matching the active pipeline. A material keeps working when a project switches pipelines, nothing to install, copy, reassign, or upgrade, and no separate URP shader menu. Detection is automatic.  Most of the package behaves identically in both. The exceptions:  Feature Built-in Universal Particles/Grab Distortion Refracts through GrabPass Needs Opaque Texture on the URP Asset Decals/Depth Volume Reads scene depth directly Needs the CrowPSX Depth Volume renderer feature Terrain/PBR Built-in Terrain add-pass and basemap shaders URP's terrain contract Additional realtime lights One ForwardAdd pass per light Looped inside the single forward pass Bakery alpha-meta Separate pass, hidden from Unity's lightmapper Folded into the single Meta pass  Under URP, depth-volume decals need the CrowPSX Depth Volume renderer feature on the active Universal Renderer, or they drift as the camera moves. Select a Depth Volume material and use the inspector's Add To Renderer action; the installation validator also reports it. Builds automatically strip the passes belonging to the pipeline you are not using, add CROWPSX_DISABLE_VARIANT_STRIPPING to turn that off.  Optional mesh-surface outlines are controlled directly from each material, including screen-fixed/world-space width, distance fade, a UV mask, sampled base-color matching, and UV4-baked smooth outline normals for closing hard-edge gaps without changing surface shading. Built-in needs no setup. URP renders only the passes its renderer asks for, so the outline needs a draw request: add CrowPSX Outline Feature to the active Universal Renderers, or put a CrowPSX Outline Support component on a camera to cover one scene without touching the project, which is how a scene can ship with working outlines.

title: Version and platform checks
text: The package documentation lists testing on Unity 2022.3, 6.0, 6.3, and 6.6. HDRP is not included. Use a Shader Model 3.5-capable target for the main surface, particle, and decal shaders.  Compatibility statements describe the creator's tested setup. Validate your exact Unity version, URP version, renderer, graphics API, and target hardware with a representative scene.

title: After changing pipelines
text: Wait for compilation and run Tools > CrowPSX > Validate Installation . Check the active Universal Renderer when using decals or outlines, and enable Opaque Texture when using URP Grab Distortion.  If generated pipeline detection falls out of step, use Tools > CrowPSX > Regenerate Pipeline Defines . See Troubleshooting for include errors and camera-depth issues.

title: Render pipelines
text: Built-in and URP compatibility, renderer features, and setup differences.

title: CrowPSX/Surface/Default
text: The full stylized non-PBR surface shader. It includes Base Texture and tint, pre/post color correction, pixel or vertex lighting, stepped lighting, final posterization, retro geometry, opaque/cutout/transparent rendering, alpha and bake-transparency maps, grunge, emission, stencil, depth, culling, queue, and instancing controls.

title: CrowPSX/Surface/Lite
text: A reduced surface variant retaining the base surface, color adjustment, lighting, retro geometry, alpha, rendering, stencil, depth, queue, and instancing controls. It omits the Default shader's grunge and emission systems and all PBR inputs.

title: CrowPSX/Surface/PBR
text: The full physically based surface variant. It adds:  Tangent-space normal mapping Metallic map and scalar response Smoothness or roughness map workflows Ambient occlusion for indirect diffuse light and reflections Height-based parallax occlusion mapping with adjustable depth, height-floor thresholding, and integer sample steps Separate or packed core PBR maps Linked core PBR UV transforms Packed-map generation from assigned separate maps Direct Specular Strength Indirect Reflection Strength Detail normal, metallic, smoothness, and roughness maps Grunge influence on color and supported PBR channels Emission  Specular Strength and Reflection Strength default to 1 and support a 0 to 4 multiplier range for deliberately exaggerated highlights and probe reflections.  PBR artistic controls use extended ranges where the shader can safely support them: Parallax Height reaches 1 , signed normal strengths reach -4 to 4 , color grading reaches 4 , direct/indirect lighting reaches 8 , and ambient/probe intensity reaches 4 . Negative normal strength inverts the tangent-space normal-map relief. The inspector marks the practical recommended limits in amber and changes the slider from aqua to amber beyond them; normal strengths use a recommended range of -2 to 2 . Normalized material data such as Metallic, Smoothness/Roughness, Ambient Occlusion, opacity, and blend weights remains constrained to 0–1 .  Packed core maps use R Metallic, G Ambient Occlusion, B Height, and A Smoothness or Roughness. Normal maps remain separate. See PBR Workflows .

title: Surface shaders
text: Choose Default, Lite, or PBR for mesh surfaces.

title: CrowPSX/Nature/Default
text: The Default surface feature set plus animated foliage wind, grunge, and emission.

title: CrowPSX/Nature/Lite
text: The reduced Lite surface feature set plus foliage wind. Use it for large amounts of simple grass, leaf cards, vines, and background plants.

title: CrowPSX/Nature/PBR
text: The full PBR surface feature set plus foliage wind, including separate or packed maps, ambient occlusion, height parallax with floor thresholding, smoothness or roughness response, linked PBR UVs, grunge, and emission.

title: Nature Wind controls
text: Wind Enabled : master switch for the deformation Wind Presets : Still, Gentle Leaves, Grass Breeze, Shrub, Tree Canopy, and Strong Wind Wind Direction : downwind heading in degrees Maximum Bend : maximum downwind rotation in degrees Sway Frequency : broad movement in cycles per second (Hz) Sway Wavelength : world-space size of the broad wind wave Gust Influence / Frequency / Wavelength : occasional smooth pulses layered on the steady wind Leaf Flutter / Frequency / Wavelength : small high-frequency rotational response Plant Variation : offsets duplicated plants so they do not move in synchronization Flex Distribution and Mask Falloff : shape how motion builds from anchored vertices toward flexible tips Anchoring Source : Local Height, Vertex Alpha, UV2 Y, or Mask Texture Anchor Height and Full Motion Height : the local Y range the Local Height source maps across, from fully anchored to fully flexible Wind Mask , Wind Mask Channel , and Invert Wind Mask : the texture, channel, and polarity used by the Mask Texture source  Nature wind rotates vertices around the anchor instead of adding a free world-space offset, so leaves and stems remain attached to the plant pivot. The optional Wind Mask texture uses its own sampler state. Realtime Forward and ShadowCaster passes use the same deformation, while Unity/Bakery meta passes keep the rest pose because baked lighting cannot represent continuous motion.

title: Nature & wind
text: Foliage variants, anchoring, sway, gusts, and leaf flutter.

title: CrowPSX/Terrain/PBR
text: A Terrain material that uses Unity TerrainLayers for albedo, normal, metallic, smoothness, and holes data. It supports Unity's standard terrain splatmap workflow, including the far-distance basemap and additional-layer rendering.  Assign a CrowPSX/Terrain/PBR material through the Terrain object's Terrain Settings > Material > Custom field. In the Built-in Render Pipeline the following supporting shaders are selected automatically by Unity and should not be assigned directly:  Hidden/CrowPSX/Terrain/AddPass for TerrainLayers beyond the first four Hidden/CrowPSX/Terrain/Base for the far-distance basemap Hidden/CrowPSX/Terrain/BaseGen for basemap generation  Under the Universal Render Pipeline the same shader follows URP's terrain contract, including its splat and basemap handling, so those hidden Built-in helpers are unused there.  Terrain materials expose CrowPSX tint, pre/post-lighting color adjustment, pixel or vertex lighting, stepped lighting, final posterization, screen-space pixel snapping, and rendering controls. TerrainLayers remain the source of layer texture data; edit them through Unity's Terrain tools. Realtime terrain shadow casting remains unsnapped. Terrain materials do not use affine texture warping, so a VR profile applies only its snap setting to them.

title: Terrain
text: TerrainLayer materials, pipeline support, and terrain-specific controls.

title: CrowPSX/Particles/Standard
text: A ParticleSystem-oriented shader with alpha, premultiplied, additive, soft-additive, multiply, hybrid-add, cutout, and opaque modes. It supports ParticleSystem vertex color, lit/self-lit response, flipbooks and manual atlases, texture arrays, secondary and mask maps, packed VFX input, color ramps, custom streams, soft particles, depth/intersection/distance fades, UV distortion, dissolve, alpha shaping, dithering, and built-in particle presets.

title: CrowPSX/Particles/Grab Distortion
text: Includes the Standard particle feature set and a GrabPass scene-distortion path for heat haze, shockwaves, and refractive VFX. Multi-Pass and legacy double-wide stereo use true scene refraction. Single Pass Instanced and Multiview use a stereo-safe particle-surface ripple fallback to prevent cross-eye sampling. GrabPass can be expensive when many materials or draw calls use it.

title: Particles
text: Standard particle effects, scene distortion, and stereo behavior.

title: CrowPSX/Decals/Depth Volume
text: A box-volume projected decal for stains, grime, graffiti, fake shadows, puddles, and overlays. It includes multiple decal blend modes, mask/channel selection, noise breakup, opacity, independent unlit and HDR-emission output, alpha shaping and clipping, dithering, edge fade, depth/thickness fade, distance fade, depth bias, culling, and stencil controls. The decal volume must intersect the receiving geometry.  The decal rebuilds its receiver from the camera depth texture, so the rendering camera has to produce one, and it never writes depth itself. Under the Universal Render Pipeline it additionally requires the CrowPSX Depth Volume renderer feature on the active Universal Renderer, which forces a snap-free depth prepass before the transparent queue. The material inspector detects a missing feature and offers an Add To Renderer action.  Unlit Strength controls the ordinary projected decal color. HDR Emission Color and HDR Emission Strength add a separate unclamped contribution that can drive bloom with an HDR camera; setting Unlit Strength to 0 creates an emission-only decal. As a screen-projected transparent effect, a depth-volume decal does not act as a realtime light or contribute to baked global illumination.  Use Normal (Alpha) for graffiti, painted markings, stickers, and ordinary colored decals. It uses standard source-over blending and is fully opaque wherever the resulting alpha is 1 ; Alpha Clip can provide hard cutout edges. Multiply is intended for dirt, soot, shadows, and stains, while the additive modes are intended for light and glow.  Depth-volume decals use Respect Blockers by default: ordinary surfaces need no stencil setup, while any surface using Block Decals prevents the decal from appearing on its visible pixels. Receiver plus Test Receivers provides an optional allow-list workflow. Receiver and blocker flags occupy separate stencil bits and can coexist.

title: Depth-volume decals
text: Depth requirements, URP setup, blending, emission, and stencil masks.

title: CrowPSX/Skybox/Procedural
text: A procedural skybox with a zenith/horizon/ground gradient, final color grading and posterization, multiple textured celestial bodies, analytic moon phases with earthshine, configurable stars, one or two cloud layers, cloud masks and lighting, transparent surroundings/skyline texture, global rotation, and independent layer motion.  The skybox preserves HDR output from exposure, celestial bodies, and glows. Posterization quantizes HDR values without clamping them to white, allowing HDR cameras, bloom, reflection probes, and environment capture to retain highlight energy. The final camera or output pipeline remains responsible for tone mapping.  Celestial textures support Texture Alpha, Brightness (Luminance), and Alpha × Brightness masking. Brightness is suitable for opaque images with black backgrounds. Alpha × Brightness preserves authored transparency while removing dark pixels inside it, and is identical to Brightness when the source texture has no alpha channel. Celestial and star texture sampling is restricted to their visible angular footprints and occupied star cells.  Cloud self-shading follows the strongest enabled above-horizon Sun or Moon. Its sampling direction accounts for light elevation on the flat cloud deck, and the Moon's contribution follows its illuminated phase.

title: Environment lighting
text: The skybox inspector carries an Environment Lighting group that keeps Lighting > Environment Lighting > Source set to Skybox while the material is the active skybox. Filter Skybox Ambient Color optionally reduces or tints the ambient probe Unity generates from the sky; the visible sky and its skybox reflections are not recolored. Auto Apply To Active Scene pushes edits to the scene as they are made, and Apply To Scene does it once on demand.  The filter affects the realtime fallback ambient probe. Baked lightmaps and manually baked Light Probes have to be rebaked to receive a revised environment color.

title: Moon phases
text: The Moon phase cycle uses 0 for New Moon, 0.25 for First Quarter, 0.5 for Full Moon, 0.75 for Last Quarter, and 1 for New Moon again. Eight inspector presets cover the intermediate crescent and gibbous phases. Terminator Rotation changes the phase orientation, Terminator Softness feathers its boundary, and Earthshine controls visibility on the unlit side. Moon glow and cloud glow follow the illuminated fraction while the complete lunar silhouette continues to occlude stars.

title: Procedural skybox
text: Environment lighting, celestial bodies, stars, clouds, and moon phases.

title: Color Adjustment
text: Pre-lighting controls affect source Albedo before direct/indirect lighting. Post-lighting controls grade the final combined output. The bake toggle determines whether pre-lighting color correction is exported through the material meta pass.

title: Lighting
text: Every lit surface, Nature and Vertex Painting shader has three Realtime Lighting Modes , plus direct and indirect intensity, ambient/probe intensity, minimum light, stepped lighting and final posterization. The Terrain shader offers Pixel and Vertex.  Pixel : lighting, falloff and shadows are all calculated per pixel, like a standard Unity material. Vertex : the classic PS1 look. All realtime lighting, including each light's falloff, is calculated at the mesh vertices and blended across the triangle. It is unshadowed by default; Main Light Shadows adds the main directional light's shadow where the pipeline allows it (see below). Vertex Hybrid : each light's shading, including PBR highlights, is calculated at the vertices, but its falloff and shadow are applied per pixel. You keep the vertex-lit look with clean light pools and crisp shadows. Each light is shadowed only by itself, so the sun's shadow never darkens a point or spot light.  Use ordinary Unity Lights. Their color, intensity, range, cone, culling mask and render mode are all respected, and no extra components, materials or setup are required.  Light limits. Vertex mode receives up to eight lights per object; CrowPSX picks the most important automatically (Important before Auto before Not Important, then the brightest and closest). On URP Forward, the URP asset's Per Object Limit for additional lights applies instead. In Vertex Hybrid, the four most important point and spot lights get per-pixel falloff and shadows; any beyond that are lit fully per vertex, like Unity's Not Important lights.  Shadows by pipeline.  Built-in URP Forward URP Forward+ / Deferred+ Pixel All lights All lights All lights Vertex Unshadowed Main light (with Main Light Shadows ) Unshadowed Vertex Hybrid All lights All lights Main light only  In Vertex mode on Built-in and URP Forward+, all eight lights are blended into one value, so a single light's shadow cannot be separated out. In Vertex Hybrid on URP Forward+ and Deferred+, point and spot lights come from CrowPSX's own light list, which has no access to URP's shadow maps.  Batching. In Vertex mode on Built-in and URP Forward+, and in Vertex Hybrid on URP Forward+, each object receives its light selection through per-renderer data. GPU instancing still works, but those objects are not batched by the SRP Batcher. URP Forward uses Unity's own light lists and keeps SRP Batcher compatibility.

title: Retro Geometry
text: Pixel snapping, affine warp, near-camera reduction, and optional snapped shadow casting. The visible VR / Stereo Comfort group provides Off, Comfort, Balanced, and Full profiles plus independent VR Snap and VR Affine strengths. Stereo rendering uses one shared snap displacement for both eyes to preserve binocular disparity across Multi-Pass, Single Pass Instanced, and Multiview.

title: Outline
text: The six mesh-surface shaders (Default, Lite, PBR, and their Vertex Painting variants) provide an optional inverted-hull silhouette. Width can stay fixed in screen pixels or use physical world units, and an optional start/end distance fade shrinks and fades it out. A UV-transformable texture mask (luminance/R/G/B/A, optionally inverted) controls where the hull appears. Match Base Color blends toward the actual sampled surface color, including the blended layer result on Vertex Painting materials. The hull follows CrowPSX vertex wobble. Disabled materials have the outline pass switched off and submit no outline draw; enabled materials add one outline draw.  The hull is never moved to a second renderer. The outline pass is ordered after the surface pass inside one material and relies on the depth that pass wrote, and nothing guarantees that ordering between two separate renderers.  Transparent surfaces cannot reliably occlude their own hull because they normally do not write depth; Opaque or Cutout is recommended. Nature is intentionally excluded: its common single-plane alpha cards need texture-silhouette dilation rather than an inverted hull.  Built-in draws the hull as part of its forward queue, the pass is tagged LightMode = Always , which that pipeline renders unconditionally and late enough to sit on top of opaque geometry. Nothing to set up.  Universal renders only the tags its passes ask for, and the hull must be drawn after the opaque queue so the geometry that should occlude it has already written depth. It therefore carries its own LightMode = CrowPSXOutline and is drawn by a CrowPSX pass at BeforeRenderingTransparents , requested one of two ways:  CrowPSX Outline Feature on a Universal Renderer covers every camera using that renderer. CrowPSX Outline Support on a camera covers one scene without touching any project asset, which is what lets a scene ship with outlines that work on import. It adds the URP-only injector at runtime and does nothing under Built-in.  Using both is safe: the feature stands down for any camera the injector already covered. The pass records both ways, so it draws under Unity 6's Render Graph and under Compatibility Mode alike, as well as on URP versions that predate Render Graph entirely. Riding one of URP's own tags instead is a tempting shortcut and does not work, SRPDefaultUnlit is requested ahead of UniversalForward , so the hull would be drawn before the geometry that occludes it and overwritten by the opaque draws that follow.  Code toggling the outline at runtime has to set both LightMode names through Material.SetShaderPassEnabled , which matches on that tag, alongside the _OutlineEnabled property.

title: Outline normals (Baked Smooth UV4)
text: Hard edges are duplicated vertices. A cube corner is three vertices at the same position, each carrying its own axis-aligned normal, so an inverted hull extrudes each face along a different axis and comes apart into disjoint quads. On screen that reads as short strokes floating near the corners while the rest of the silhouette is missing. Rounded meshes hide the problem, because a smooth normal field still closes the hull.  Smoothing the mesh's own normals would fix the hull and flatten the shading with it. Normal Source > Baked Smooth UV4 instead uses a second set of normals that only the outline pass reads.  What the bake produces. CrowPSX copies the mesh, groups vertices that share a position, averages their distinct normals, and writes the result to UV4, TEXCOORD3 in the shaders. Welding is positional, with a tolerance scaled to the mesh bounds. Positions, lighting normals, vertex colors and lightmap UVs are untouched, so shading is unchanged; the extra channel is read only while Normal Source is set to Baked Smooth UV4, and ignored everywhere else.  How the normal is stored. Not as an object-space direction, but as coordinates in each vertex's own tangent frame, flagged by w = 2 . Static batching and GPU skinning rewrite NORMAL and TANGENT into another space while copying UV channels through verbatim, so a direction parked in UV4 would quietly stop matching the geometry it belongs to the moment either applied. Tangent-frame coordinates travel with the basis and stay correct in both cases. Tangents are generated on the generated copy when the source mesh has none, since the encoding needs them; a vertex whose tangent is still unusable falls back to an object-space direction flagged w = 1 , which the shaders also read, that is the encoding meshes baked before this change carry, and the inspector flags them so they can be baked again.  Baking and restoring. In the material inspector, Source Renderer defaults to the selected object's renderer and only appears while Normal Source is Baked Smooth UV4. Bake Outline Normals bakes that renderer in place: the generated mesh is assigned to it and its materials are switched to Baked Smooth UV4. Restore Source Mesh puts the recorded original back without deleting the generated asset. Below the buttons the section reports which mesh is being drawn, or warns that it has no UV4 or carries the older encoding. Tools > CrowPSX > Outline Normals runs the same two actions across every MeshFilter and SkinnedMeshRenderer under the current selection.  Generated assets. Each mesh is written beside its source model as <model>_<mesh>_OutlineNormals.asset . Two labels record the original mesh reference and the source's dependency hash. Restore resolves the original through the first; re-baking reuses the existing asset when both still match, and updates that same asset in place when the model changed, so bake/restore cycles never accumulate numbered duplicates.  Requirements and limits. Meshes need Read/Write enabled in the model importer. Only imported mesh assets can be baked: the generated copy is saved beside its source model, so a scene-only or procedural mesh has nowhere to be written and no stable identity for Restore to resolve, and the baker refuses it rather than putting the asset somewhere else. Welding is purely positional, so surfaces that merely touch are averaged together, which closes the hull across them whether or not that was intended.

title: Rendering
text: Opaque/Cutout/Transparent modes; source alpha and separate Alpha Map; Bake Transparency Map; alpha contrast/power/bias, clipping, and dithering; Cull, Z Write, Z Test, depth bias, queue, stencil, and GPU instancing.

title: Grunge and Emission
text: Available only on shaders that declare the corresponding properties. The inspector hides unsupported sections automatically.  The Grunge layer and the Grunge Mask each choose a Projection Type , presented the same way as the Depth Volume decal's:  Type Cost Behavior UV 1 fetch Follows the mesh texture coordinates. The default. Planar 1 fetch Projects from one direction (X, Y, or Z). Surfaces facing away from it stretch. Biplanar 2 fetches Blends the selected pair (XY, XZ, or YZ) using the surface normal. Triplanar 3 fetches Blends all three directions using the surface normal.  Planar and Biplanar sample only their enabled axes, so they are genuinely cheaper than Triplanar rather than Triplanar with some weights zeroed. Projection Blend Sharpness applies to Biplanar and Triplanar only; Planar has nothing to blend between. Use Local Position stays available in every mode, because the breakup and streak noise are driven from that position even under UV mapping.  Grunge follows height parallax in every projection type. UV mapping follows it through the displaced texture coordinates; the projected types are addressed by position instead, so parallax additionally publishes its displacement in world space and the projection position picks it up. This also covers the breakup and streak noise, which are position-addressed even under UV mapping.

title: Lighting & retro controls
text: Lighting modes, vertex snapping, affine warp, outlines, and rendering.

title: Surface response workflow
text: Choose Smoothness or Roughness in Surface Response Workflow .  Smoothness describes how polished the surface is. White is smooth and black is rough. Roughness describes how microscopically uneven the surface is. White is rough and black is smooth.  The response value works without a texture and multiplies the selected map when one is assigned. Packed maps store the selected response in alpha; changing the workflow changes how that alpha channel is interpreted.

title: Separate and packed maps
text: PBR Map Workflow offers two layouts:  Separate Maps uses independent Metallic, Ambient Occlusion, Height, and Smoothness or Roughness textures. Choose it when the maps need different resolutions, import settings, or UV transforms. Packed Map combines the grayscale PBR data in one linear texture. Choose it to reduce texture sampling and keep the maps synchronized.  Normal maps remain separate in both workflows and must be imported as Unity Normal Map textures. Normal Strength and Detail Normal Strength accept -4 to 4 ; negative values invert the map's tangent-space relief. -1 gives the equal-and-opposite relief of 1 , while 0 disables that map's influence. The recommended working range is -2 to 2 .  The packed channel layout is:  Channel Data R Metallic G Ambient Occlusion B Height A Smoothness or Roughness, according to the material workflow  Packed PBR textures are data textures. Disable sRGB sampling when importing a packed map manually. The built-in packing tool configures this automatically.

title: Build a packed PBR map
text: When PBR Map Workflow is set to Separate Maps , the inspector places a themed Build Packed PBR Map card directly below the workflow description. The card previews the output channels before any asset is created:  Assign the separate Metallic, Ambient Occlusion, Height, and Smoothness or Roughness maps you want to pack. Select the correct Surface Response Workflow . Regular PBR response maps use red; painted layers can select red or alpha for their separate response map. Press Review Packed Map Creation → . Review the save, assignment, and workflow-switch summary. Press Create & Switch to Packed , or choose Not Now to cancel.  CrowPSX creates a linear PNG beside the Base Texture when it is a project asset, or beside the material when no project texture is assigned. It assigns the new texture and changes PBR Map Workflow to Packed Map . Separate-map references remain intact, so switching back does not discard the setup. If detail maps are enabled on a regular Surface or Nature PBR material, the tool also creates and assigns the matching Detail Packed PBR map.  The output resolution follows the largest assigned source map, up to 4096 pixels per dimension. The packed map inherits the Metallic map's UV transform; enable linked UVs first when all source maps should use the same transform.

title: Linked PBR UVs
text: Enable Link PBR UVs when the core PBR maps should follow the surface-color texture's tiling, offset, rotation, and scrolling. The surface-color UV controls become the shared transform and individual core-map transforms are hidden.  Disable the option when a map needs its own transform. Detail maps always keep independent UV controls.

title: Ambient occlusion
text: Ambient Occlusion uses the red channel of a separate AO map or the green channel of a packed map. Ambient Occlusion Strength blends between no occlusion and the texture value.  AO affects indirect diffuse light and reflections. It does not replace realtime shadows and does not darken direct light from the main or additional lights.

title: Height and parallax
text: Height maps produce view-dependent surface relief by offsetting texture coordinates; they do not move mesh vertices or change the object's silhouette.  Separate maps read height from red. Packed maps read height from blue. White represents raised detail and black represents recessed detail. Parallax Height controls the depth of the effect. Its full authoring range is 0–1 , while 0.1 is the recommended maximum for ordinary materials. Start near zero and increase gradually. Height Floor sets the minimum level of the height map. 0 uses the complete map unchanged. Raising the floor lifts recessed areas toward the peaks and compresses the relief range upward; 1 produces a flat height field at the highest level. Parallax Steps is an integer from 1 to 64. Higher values reduce visible stepping at grazing angles but require more height-map samples. Values above 32 are marked amber because their cost is usually best reserved for close-up materials. Values below 4 are intentionally available for very low-cost or strongly stylized materials and can show obvious stepping.  Parallax is most convincing on surfaces viewed at moderate angles with a consistent tangent basis. CrowPSX bounds and fades displacement at extreme grazing angles to keep high values stable, but very large height values, mirrored tangents, or mismatched map UVs can still stretch the texture. It cannot create true overhangs or silhouette displacement.  Parallax Steps is a total sample budget at grazing angles, not a fixed per-pixel cost. The ray march spends it on a linear search that brackets the surface, then a bisection pass that locates the hit inside that bracket. The linear pass takes about half and saturates at 16, since past that point extra linear samples only guard against stepping over a thin feature; bisection takes what is left, up to four. Each halving narrows the result twice as far for one sample, which the linear pass would need double its budget to match.  The split comes out of the budget rather than being added to it, so the setting is never more expensive than the number implies:  Parallax Steps Linear Bisection Total samples 1–3 1–3 0 1–3 4 3 1 4 8 4 4 8 12 6 4 10 32 16 4 20 64 16 4 20  Two further effects scale the real cost down from there. A pixel whose total displacement works out below half a pixel skips the march entirely, which covers most distant geometry. Everything else scales both budgets by how far from head-on it is viewed, since a surface seen straight on has almost no displacement to resolve.  High Steps values therefore cost far less than the number suggests, and resolve more precisely than the same count spent purely on linear samples. Budgets of 3 or below spend everything on the linear pass.

title: Grunge height
text: On PBR shaders, the Grunge layer can optionally influence height as well as surface color and response. Positive Height Influence embosses the grunge pattern; negative values carve it into the surface. This is independent of the base Height map, follows the Grunge mask and blend weight, and only affects parallax when both Grunge Height and the material's parallax are active.  Grunge Height is the one Grunge response that is evaluated inside the parallax ray march rather than once per pixel, because a height field has to be resampled at every marched step to produce relief. Its cost therefore scales with Parallax Steps , multiplied again by the Grunge Projection Type: three texture fetches per step under Triplanar, two under Biplanar, one under UV or Planar. Two settings dominate beyond that. Vertical Streaking at zero skips its noise entirely, so leaving it at zero when you do not want streaks is free performance. The projection type matters more than it looks: Triplanar evaluates 3D noise, which costs twice as much per octave as the 2D noise the UV and Planar paths use.  The march probes a reduced-detail version of the grunge (the low-frequency octaves, rescaled to the same range and mean as the full set so the field is smoother rather than shallower) while shading still reads it at full detail. The relief is therefore resolved against a slightly smoother field than the one you see, which costs roughly half as much per step and is not visible at ordinary Height Influence values.  If Grunge Height is still too expensive: drop the projection to Planar, set Vertical Streaking to zero, lower Parallax Steps, or drive height from the base Height map and leave Grunge on color and response only, which avoids the cost entirely.  Extended artistic sliders show amber markers at their recommended limits and turn amber after crossing them. Values beyond those markers are valid and intentionally available for exaggerated materials, but they are more likely to expose artifacts or produce non-neutral lighting. Normal-strength controls use a signed recommended range of -2 to 2 . Physically normalized controls such as Metallic, Smoothness/Roughness, Ambient Occlusion, opacity, and blend weights remain limited to 0–1 .

title: Detail maps
text: Detail maps add close-range microstructure independently of the core PBR maps. Detail Normal remains separate. Metallic and surface response can use separate detail maps or the detail packed map, where red stores Metallic and alpha stores Smoothness or Roughness.  Use detail maps only where the extra samples are useful, such as fine scratches, pores, worn shine, or micro-normal noise.

title: Runtime and compilation behavior
text: PBR Map Workflow, Surface Response Workflow, detail-map use, grunge, and emission are material controls rather than separate CrowPSX shader-feature variants. Changing these controls does not create a new combination of CrowPSX PBR programs. Unity still provides its normal Built-in Render Pipeline variants for lighting, shadows, fog, instancing, and lightmapping.  Disabled systems avoid their expensive work. A Parallax Height of 0 skips parallax traversal, Ambient Occlusion Strength of 0 skips separate AO reads, zero direct or indirect intensity skips the corresponding lighting work, and zero specular or reflection strength skips its BRDF or reflection-probe contribution. In packed mode, one RGBA sample supplies Metallic, Ambient Occlusion, and Smoothness/Roughness for the visible surface or painted layer. Height uses the same packed asset during parallax traversal.  Vertex-painted PBR evaluates only layers that contribute visible weight at the current pixel or vertex. Solid Base, Red, Green, or Blue regions therefore avoid reading the other three layers; transition regions evaluate the layers participating in the blend. Zero-weight layers also cannot activate the shared parallax loop. Packed maps remain the preferred layout when several painted layers overlap or parallax is enabled.

title: Vertex-painted PBR
text: CrowPSX/Surface/Vertex Painting/PBR gives Base, Red, Green, and Blue their own:  Separate or Packed Map workflow Smoothness or Roughness workflow Linked or independent PBR UVs Albedo, normal strength, metallic, AO, height/parallax, and surface-response values  This allows one material to mix workflows; for example, Base and Red can use packed maps while Green uses separate maps. Parallax Height and Height Floor are set independently per layer, while Parallax Steps is shared by all four layers.  Separate Maps is the heaviest vertex-painted PBR setup because every active layer can sample albedo, normal, metallic, response, AO, and height independently. Prefer packed maps for runtime-heavy painted materials and use low parallax step counts unless grazing-angle quality requires more.  Each painted layer displays its own Pack Base/Red/Green/Blue Layer card immediately below that layer's workflow control. Its review and confirmation buttons create, assign, and switch only that layer to Packed Map .

title: PBR workflows
text: Map layouts, packing, surface response, UVs, parallax, and detail.

title: CrowPSX/Surface/Vertex Painting/Default
text: Four Albedo layers, each with a Tint and independent UV transform, plus compatible Default lighting, retro, rendering, grunge, and emission controls.

title: CrowPSX/Surface/Vertex Painting/Lite
text: Four Albedo layers with Tint and UV controls, using the reduced Lite feature set.

title: CrowPSX/Surface/Vertex Painting/PBR
text:
Four PBR layers. Every Base, Red, Green, and Blue layer independently chooses Separate Maps or Packed Map and Smoothness or Roughness. Each layer contains:  Albedo texture, Tint, and UV transform Normal texture, signed Normal Strength ( -4 to 4 ), and UV transform Metallic texture, Metallic Strength, and UV transform Ambient Occlusion texture and strength Height texture, Parallax Height, and per-layer Height Floor Smoothness/Roughness texture, Red/Alpha channel selection, response value, and UV transform Optional linked PBR UVs driven by that layer's Albedo transform  Packed painted maps use R Metallic, G Ambient Occlusion, B Height, and A Smoothness or Roughness. The inspector can generate a packed texture from the active layer's separate maps. The same normalized layer weights blend Albedo, Normal, Metallic, Ambient Occlusion, Height, surface response, and texture alpha. Parallax Height is per layer and the integer Parallax Steps setting is shared across all layers.  All maps in one painted layer share that layer's Albedo sampler state to stay inside D3D11 sampler limits. They can use separate UV transforms, but their texture filtering and wrap behavior should be compatible. Separate Maps can be expensive when several painted layers contribute at once; packed maps are recommended for runtime-heavy materials.  See Vertex Painting .  CrowPSX includes three dedicated four-layer vertex-painting shaders:  CrowPSX/Surface/Vertex Painting/Default
CrowPSX/Surface/Vertex Painting/Lite
CrowPSX/Surface/Vertex Painting/PBR

title: Layer weights
text:
The mesh vertex-color channels are interpreted as:  R = Red layer
G = Green layer
B = Blue layer
A = Base layer  CrowPSX normalizes the four weights. If all channels are zero, the shader falls back to the Base layer. Layer Blend Strength fades the painted result toward Base. Layer Blend Sharpness increases or softens dominance at transitions.

title: Polybrush setup
text: Polybrush is optional. For predictable four-layer splat painting, use Texture Paint rather than ordinary unrestricted Color Paint.  CrowPSX writes recommended texture-paint metadata automatically. If Polybrush displays a texture-blending warning, run:  Tools > CrowPSX > Polybrush > Configure Texture Painting  Then reselect the object or leave and re-enter Texture Paint mode. The generated layout maps Base to alpha, then Red, Green, and Blue to their matching vertex channels.

title: Mesh requirements
text: Painting resolution is limited by mesh vertex density. A quad with four vertices can only store values at its corners. Subdivide the mesh or author sufficient topology for the desired brush detail.  The mesh and any optimization/combination pipeline must preserve vertex colors. Paint a duplicate before applying destructive mesh operations.

title: Vertex lighting and local lights
text: CrowPSX Vertex mode follows Unity's native Gouraud path. The ForwardBase main light and the Built-in VERTEXLIGHT_ON list are evaluated at mesh vertices and interpolated across the surface.  In the Built-in pipeline, set local point and spot lights to Not Important to place them in that native vertex-light list. Unity represents those lights as unshadowed point lights there. Auto and Important lights arrive as ForwardAdd pixel lights and are still vertex evaluated in pure Vertex mode; point and spot lights there get a narrow per-fragment envelope so Unity's rectangular ForwardAdd bounds never show.  Prefer Not Important when you want the classic look. Unity scissors a ForwardAdd pass to the light's bounds, so an Auto or Important light cannot spill past its range volume no matter how large the triangles are, the envelope hides the hard box edge but cannot render outside it. A Not Important light is evaluated in ForwardBase alongside the rest of the mesh, so its interpolated falloff carries across the whole triangle. Use Vertex Hybrid when those lights need their normal falloff, cookies, or realtime shadows.  Vertex density controls the result: a local light only affects a triangle when it reaches one or more of that triangle's vertices.  Main Light Shadows optionally samples the Built-in ForwardBase main light's shadow per fragment. It does not add shadows to native vertex point or spot lights.

title: Default and Lite layers
text: Each Base/Red/Green/Blue layer contains:  Albedo texture Tint Independent Albedo tiling, offset, rotation, and scrolling  These shaders do not use regular _MainTex or _Tint properties.

title: PBR layers
text: Each Base/Red/Green/Blue layer independently selects its PBR Map Workflow , Surface Response Workflow , and Link PBR UVs option. A material can mix packed and separate layers as needed.

title: Albedo
text: Texture, Tint, and UV transform. When Link PBR UVs is enabled, this transform controls all core PBR maps in the layer.

title: Normal
text: Normal texture, signed Normal Strength, and independent UV transform. Import the asset as a Unity Normal Map . Strength accepts -4 to 4 : negative values invert the map's tangent-space relief, 0 disables its influence, and the recommended range is -2 to 2 . The CrowPSX inspector shows a Fix action for an incorrect import type.

title: Metallic
text: Metallic texture, Metallic Strength, and independent UV transform. The texture uses its red channel. The scalar is used directly when no map is assigned and multiplies the map when present.

title: Surface response
text: Choose Smoothness or Roughness independently for each layer. The response texture supports Red or Alpha channel selection and an independent UV transform. The scalar is used directly when no map is assigned and multiplies the selected channel when present.

title: Ambient occlusion
text: The separate AO map uses its red channel. Ambient Occlusion Strength blends between no occlusion and the texture and affects indirect diffuse light and reflections.

title: Height and parallax
text: The separate Height map uses its red channel. Parallax Height controls view-dependent UV relief for that layer; it does not displace vertices or alter the silhouette. Every layer supports 0–1 , with 0.1 marked as the recommended maximum for normal use. Height Floor is also independent per layer: 0 uses the complete map, while higher values raise that layer's minimum height and lift recessed areas toward the peaks. A floor of 1 produces a flat height field at the highest level. Parallax Steps is an integer from 1 to 64 and is shared by all four layers; values above 32 receive an amber performance warning, while values below 4 trade visible stepping for lower sampling cost.

title: Packed maps
text: Packed Map uses R Metallic, G Ambient Occlusion, B Height, and A Smoothness or Roughness. Normal remains separate. The channel guide in the material inspector follows the selected response workflow.  In Separate Maps mode, each layer shows a themed Pack Base/Red/Green/Blue Layer card directly below its workflow control. Press Review Packed Map Creation → , review the channel and save summary, then choose Create & Switch to Packed . CrowPSX creates a linear PNG beside that layer's Albedo texture when possible, otherwise beside the material. It assigns the map and switches only that layer to Packed Map; the separate-map references are retained. Choose Not Now to leave the material unchanged.

title: Linked PBR UVs
text: Enable Link PBR UVs to make the layer's Albedo tiling, offset, rotation, and scrolling control its Normal, Metallic, response, AO, Height, and Packed maps. Disable it when individual transforms are required.

title: Sampler-state limitation
text: The PBR painted shader can sample several texture families across four layers. To remain below D3D11 pixel-shader sampler limits, all maps in one layer share that layer's Albedo sampler state. They can still have separate textures and UV transforms, but should use compatible filtering and wrap settings within a layer.  Separate Maps is the heaviest painted-PBR workflow because an active layer can independently sample Albedo, Normal, Metallic, surface response, AO, and Height. Prefer Packed Map on runtime-heavy materials. Higher Parallax Steps also increase the number of height samples.  CrowPSX skips map reads for painted layers whose normalized weight is zero. Solid single-layer areas therefore evaluate only that layer, while blended transitions evaluate each layer that visibly contributes. Setting a layer's Normal Strength, Ambient Occlusion Strength, or Parallax Height to 0 also skips the corresponding optional map work. Packed/separate selection remains independent per layer and is resolved at runtime rather than creating every possible four-layer shader combination.

title: Alpha, shadows, and baking
text: Layer texture alpha is blended with the same vertex weights. It can feed Cutout or Transparent rendering and is used by compatible shadow and meta passes. A painted fence, leaf, or damaged surface can therefore produce a layer-dependent cutout silhouette.

title: Brush strokes follow large triangles
text: The mesh needs more vertices.

title: The material stays on Base
text: Confirm that the painted shader is assigned, the mesh has vertex colors, Polybrush is editing the rendered mesh, and Layer Blend Strength is above zero.

title: Unexpected colors or base leakage
text: Inspect the RGBA weights. Texture Paint is recommended because it maintains a clearer normalized layer workflow than arbitrary Color Paint values.

title: Polybrush says vertex colors or texture blending are unsupported
text: Reimport the painted shader, run the CrowPSX Polybrush configuration command, and reselect the object so Polybrush refreshes its compatibility check.

title: Vertex painting
text: Four-layer painting, layer maps, Polybrush integration, and painted PBR.

title: Target sources
text: The Batch workspace can collect materials from:  Selection Scene Surfaces Scene All Scene Particles Scene Decals Scene CrowPSX All Project Surfaces Project All Project Particles Project Decals Project CrowPSX All  Selection can optionally include child renderers. The resulting target list can be searched, filtered, sorted, added to, replaced, or reduced manually.

title: Copy from source
text: Copies compatible settings from one source material to the target list. Guided scopes include Recommended, Appearance, Appearance and Textures, Everything, and Custom. The Custom scope can select schema groups and value types. Unsupported destination properties are skipped.

title: Reset defaults
text: Resets selected groups to the actual defaults of each destination shader variant. Texture slots are preserved unless texture reset is explicitly included. Use Full Reset carefully.

title: Convert variant
text: Converts compatible surfaces among:  Default Lite PBR Vertex Painting · Default Vertex Painting · Lite Vertex Painting · PBR  Particles, decals, skyboxes, and special CrowPSX shaders are protected from surface conversion. Compatible values are preserved when requested. Conversion between regular and painted variants preserves Base-layer data where possible, but cannot invent meaningful Red/Green/Blue layers.

title: Apply preset
text: Applies a built-in or custom preset using a selected scope. Custom presets are shared with the material inspector and stored in:  ProjectSettings/CrowPSX/CustomMaterialPresets.json

title: Rendering and lighting
text: Batch-change Opaque/Cutout/Transparent rendering, Pixel/Vertex lighting, or both. CrowPSX then validates render tags, blend state, queue, keywords, and recommended depth behavior.

title: VR profile
text: Applies a consistent VR comfort profile across compatible target materials. Off , Comfort , Balanced , and Full provide immediate starting points; Custom exposes separate snap and affine strengths. Terrain materials receive the snap setting and ignore affine strength because the Terrain shader does not use affine texture warping.  VR profiles only scale the existing retro effects during stereo rendering. They do not change the material's desktop Pixel Snap or Affine Warp values. Stereo snapping uses a shared displacement for both eyes in Multi-Pass, Single Pass Instanced, and Multiview.

title: Target-list performance
text: Scene usage is cached and invalidated after hierarchy, project, selection, or Undo changes. Large target lists are virtualized. Project-wide collection still scans project Material assets and can take time in large projects.

title: Safe workflow
text: Commit or back up the project. Choose the narrowest target source. Review and filter the target list. Start with a conservative scope. Apply the operation. Review the report and inspect representative materials. Use Unity Undo immediately when the result is not intended.  Test project-wide conversions on a copy of the project first.

title: Material Manager
text: Batch targets, presets, conversion, rendering, checks, and themes.

title: Opaque materials
text: Opaque materials cast a solid geometric silhouette. Their baked Albedo comes from the regular surface or blended painted layers, Tint, and the bake-color controls exposed by the inspector.

title: Cutout materials
text: Cutout uses the selected alpha source and Alpha Cutoff to decide which pixels exist. With a compatible lightmapper, a fence, grate, leaf card, or torn surface can bake a cutout-shaped shadow instead of the complete rectangular polygon.  Recommended setup:  Rendering Mode = Cutout Correct texture-alpha or Alpha Map source enabled Alpha Cutoff matched to the realtime silhouette Renderer Cast Shadows enabled Z Write enabled for ordinary cutout materials Light and receiver included in the bake

title: Alpha sources
text: Depending on the shader, opacity can use:  Base Texture alpha Blended painted-layer alpha Separate Alpha Map with selectable channel Alpha contrast, power, and bias Optional final alpha clip or dither

title: Bake Transparency Map
text: The optional Bake Transparency Map is a Bakery-only override. Use it when Bakery should bake a silhouette that differs from the rendered opacity. Black is opaque and white transmits light; CrowPSX converts it to opacity for the Bakery alpha-meta output.  Unity's Progressive Lightmapper does not read that map. It resolves transparency itself, from the base texture's alpha and the base color, and that is enough for the great majority of materials.

title: Why there is no transmission texture to manage
text: Unity's lightmapper offers two transparency paths, and a shader picks one by what it declares:  Monochrome (default). Unity reads the alpha of _MainTex and _Color . CrowPSX provides both ( _Color is kept in sync with the Tint) so this works with no setup and no generated assets. RGB transmission. Declaring a _TransparencyLM texture property switches the shader to a texture-based path, which supports colored transmission.  CrowPSX deliberately does not declare _TransparencyLM , because that choice is per shader rather than per material. Declaring it opts every material into the texture path, and that path has no empty state: a material left with an empty slot is not treated as opaque, it fails to export, and the object then contributes nothing to the bake, no emission, no shadow even at full opacity, and no indirect light until it is switched back to Opaque. Supporting colored transmission for the few materials that want it would mean generating and maintaining a transmission texture for every transparent material in the project.  The one consequence worth knowing: the separate Alpha Map is invisible to Unity's lightmapper , since Unity only reads _MainTex alpha and never runs the shader. Bakery sees it correctly through the Meta pass. If a Unity bake needs that silhouette, composite the alpha map into the base texture's alpha channel.

title: Bakery
text: Compatible surface shaders include a META_BAKERY pass and BAKERY_META_ALPHA_ENABLE in both pipelines. This covers the Surface, Vertex Painting, and Nature families; the Terrain, particle, decal, and skybox shaders have no Bakery path in either pipeline.  CrowPSX supplies the material-side alpha output only. Bakery settings, light contribution, lightmap resolution, renderer settings, whether your Bakery version supports the active render pipeline, and the Bakery version itself all still determine the result.

title: Realtime Global Illumination
text:
Unity's Enlighten realtime GI works in the Built-in Render Pipeline and is not available under
the Universal Render Pipeline , which removed it. A scene authored with it will lose that
contribution when opened in URP.  Watch for Realtime Environment Lighting in particular: with it enabled the environment is
carried by the realtime GI data instead of the baked lightmap, so under URP the ambient fill
disappears and shadows go black. Bake with Realtime Global Illumination disabled for scenes
that have to work in both pipelines.

title: Mixed lighting
text: All three of Unity's mixed lighting modes work on Surface, Vertex Painting, and Nature materials in both render pipelines.  Baked Indirect : the lightmap carries indirect only, and every shadow is realtime. Nothing is shadowed past the shadow distance. Shadowmask : realtime shadows near the camera hand over to baked shadows from the shadowmask texture at the shadow distance. Mixed lights also take their baked occlusion from that texture. Subtractive : the lightmap carries the full baked result and the main light's direct contribution is subtracted back out where it is shadowed.  The Terrain shader supports the same three modes.

title: Painted materials
text: Painted variants export blended layer Albedo and alpha to compatible shadow and meta paths. Different painted layers can therefore contribute different cutout patterns and baked colors.

title: Emission
text: Supported shaders export unclamped HDR Emission through the meta pass when enabled. Strong realtime glow alone does not guarantee strong baked contribution; the renderer must contribute GI, the material must be marked Baked Emissive, and the lightmapper must have Baked Global Illumination enabled.

title: Matching realtime and baked alpha
text: Use the same alpha path for realtime and baking when possible. Match Alpha Cutoff to the desired silhouette. Avoid extreme alpha shaping until the baked result is tested. Give the receiving surface enough lightmap resolution. Re-bake after changing alpha textures, import settings, UVs, cutoff, or rendering mode.

title: Baking & transparency
text: Alpha, lightmapping, Bakery integration, and transparency controls.

title: Supported modes
text: Supported across every shader family: Multi-Pass, Single Pass Instanced, and Android Multiview in the Built-in Render Pipeline, and Single Pass Instanced and Multiview under URP.  Retro geometry uses stereo-stable snapping, both eyes receive the same screen-space displacement, preserving binocular disparity instead of quantizing each eye independently. The material inspector exposes a VR / Stereo Comfort group with profiles and separate snap and affine strengths, and the Material Manager can apply them in bulk.  Two Built-in-only notes: deferred rendering does not support Single Pass Instanced, so use Forward for that mode, and Grab Distortion falls back to a stereo-safe surface ripple outside Multi-Pass.

title: Configure a material
text: CrowPSX supports Multi-Pass, Single Pass Instanced, and Android Multiview in the Built-in Render Pipeline, and URP's Single Pass Instanced and Multiview modes.  Use the Forward rendering path for Single Pass Instanced. Built-in deferred does not support that mode. Soft particles and Depth Volume decals require the camera depth texture. Grab Distortion uses true scene refraction in Multi-Pass and a stereo-safe heat-ripple fallback in Single Pass Instanced/Multiview. Use VR / Stereo Comfort to choose a profile or tune VR Snap Strength and VR Affine Strength independently. Stereo snapping shares one displacement between both eyes to preserve binocular disparity.

title: Apply a profile in bulk
text: Applies a consistent VR comfort profile across compatible target materials. Off , Comfort , Balanced , and Full provide immediate starting points; Custom exposes separate snap and affine strengths. Terrain materials receive the snap setting and ignore affine strength because the Terrain shader does not use affine texture warping.  VR profiles only scale the existing retro effects during stereo rendering. They do not change the material's desktop Pixel Snap or Affine Warp values. Stereo snapping uses a shared displacement for both eyes in Multi-Pass, Single Pass Instanced, and Multiview.

title: VR & stereo
text: Supported stereo modes, comfort controls, and rendering limitations.

title: Controls
text:
WASD : move Mouse : look Left Shift : sprint Space : jump F : toggle the flashlight Tab : show/hide the controls list V : noclip  The controls list fades once the player begins moving and hands over to a subtle
bottom bar: a black gradient carrying the key prompts on the right and, whenever
the player looks at a CrowPSXInspectableObject , that object's description on the left.

title: Outlines under URP
text:
The demo camera carries a CrowPSX Outline Support component. Under URP the
outline is a separate pass that the renderer has to be told to draw, and the usual
way to do that (a renderer feature) lives in a project asset that a scene cannot
bring with it. The component makes the same request per camera instead, so the demo
shows its outlines as soon as the scene is opened, in any URP project, with nothing
configured. Under Built-in it does nothing and can stay where it is.

title: Input and UI requirements
text: The sample scripts work with any Active Input Handling setting. They use the legacy Input Manager when it is enabled, and read the keyboard and mouse through the Input System when it is the only backend, which is the default for new Unity 6 projects. Nothing needs to be changed in Player Settings to run the demo.  The controls overlay uses Unity UI ( com.unity.ugui ), which is included in standard Unity 2022.3 and Unity 6 projects. The CrowPSX shaders themselves do not depend on the sample controller or Unity UI.

title: Sample scripts
text:
The reusable demo scripts are under Assets/CrowPSX/Samples/Scripts in the CrowPSX.Samples namespace:  CrowPSXFirstPersonMovement CrowPSXMouseLook CrowPSXHeadBob CrowPSXFootstepSystem CrowPSXStaminaSystem CrowPSXPlayerHUD CrowPSXInspectableObject CrowPSXTransformPath CrowPSXLightingModeTester  CrowPSXTransformPath moves an object through a list of waypoint Transforms, carrying rotation and optional scale at each one. It was built to sweep a lamp across a wall of materials: timing is either a constant speed, so a long leg takes proportionally longer and the light never appears to accelerate between segments, or a fixed number of seconds per segment when the beats matter more than the pace. It also offers smoothed or straight-line paths, Once/Loop/PingPong looping, per-segment easing, and a dwell time at each waypoint.  CrowPSXPlayerHUD builds the whole HUD in code - no canvas to wire up - and takes the
JetBrains Mono fonts from Assets/CrowPSX/Editor/Font . Add CrowPSXInspectableObject to anything you want described: write its Title and Details , and the HUD
prints them in a bordered box in the bottom-left corner, with a thin leader line
running from the box to the object itself. The box grows to fit the text. One component
covers a whole hierarchy - put it on the root of a multi-mesh prop and looking at
any child reads out the same thing. A child with its own CrowPSXInspectableObject overrides the parent, and Include Children turns the inheritance off. The object
needs a collider to be looked at; a trigger works as well as a solid one.  CrowPSXInspectableObject also switches on the CrowPSX outline of its own renderers
while the player is looking at it, on the same detection that drives the readout. Highlight Outline turns the behavior off per object. The component instances
that object's materials at startup and enables their outline pass with the outline
itself switched off, so a prop can ship with no outline in the project and still
light up when seen; the project's material assets are never modified. With Override Outline Look on it draws in Highlight Color and Highlight Width ,
and with it off the material's own outline color and width are used instead. Props
whose shader has no outline (terrain, skybox, particles, decals) simply never
highlight.  CrowPSXLightingModeTester shows one set of CrowPSX materials at a chosen realtime
lighting mode without authoring a duplicate material per mode. It clones the
materials on the renderers it drives, so the source assets are never modified.  They are demonstration components rather than a required runtime dependency of the shader package.
